measurement.happened:
This week in Indonesia was dominated by a political earthquake of the highest order, layered over a worsening environmental crisis and a noisy but mixed economic picture.

THE VICE-PRESIDENTIAL RESIGNATION AND THE END OF THE JOKOWI-PRABOWO ALLIANCE. The single biggest story was the resignation of Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 36-year-old son of former President Jokowi. The sequence unfolded rapidly: on November 10, a presidential official confirmed Gibran expressed his intention to step down during talks with President Prabowo (Reuters, Bloomberg, Financial Times). On November 11, multiple sources confirmed the resignation was being formalized (Reuters, AP, Al Jazeera). On November 12, Gibran handed his resignation letter to parliament, and Prabowo formally accepted it (Reuters, Bloomberg, AP, BBC, TV5Monde, Al Jazeera). The trigger was a public dispute over his academic credentials and eligibility for the vice-presidency; 120 lawmakers immediately filed an impeachment motion over his education qualifications (AP, Reuters). The BBC framed it as a sign that the ruling alliance between Prabowo and the still-popular former President Jokowi was fraying. Bloomberg was more blunt: Prabowo was 'rushing the end of the Jokowi era' by ousting his son. The upper house (DPD) will select a new vice president on December 2 (Reuters). The resignation shattered what had been a powerful political compact, and the FT warned the wiretapping scandal now threatens 'open warfare' among the political elite. TV5Monde noted that social media posts were misrepresenting a protest salute as support for a rival of Prabowo, adding to the noise around the episode.

THE WIETAPPING SCANDAL AND TREASON CHARGES. Running parallel to the VP drama was the fallout from the illegal wiretapping of President Prabowo and others. On November 12, the police chief stated that the illegal wiretapping extended to many people beyond the president, and that police had enough evidence to pursue treason charges in the Prabowo wiretapping case (Reuters, AP). Bloomberg reported that the ex-police chief was alleged to be the 'end user' of the wiretaps. The Financial Times called it a scandal threatening 'open warfare' among Indonesia's political elite. Deutsche Welle described it as opening a political fault line. On November 9, Reuters reported that Indonesia was considering bug sweeps and tighter controls on spy tools in the aftermath. This scandal is now deeply entangled with the VP resignation, as both stories feed a narrative of a Prabowo government consolidating power while its internal alliances crack.

WILDFIRES, CLIMATE, AND THE HUMAN TOLL. The environmental crisis was the week's other major theme. A study published this week found that climate change and El Niño supercharged the fires, which burned through nearly 2.9 million hectares (Reuters, AFP, Bloomberg). An AFP report stated that fire pollution killed 3,560 people in September alone. Scientists confirmed that climate change made the fires more severe (Reuters). The government moved to revoke land rights of eight listed firms for their alleged involvement in the wildfires (Reuters). Bloomberg noted that palm oil prices climbed on fears El Niño threatens 2027 supplies. Deutsche Welle reported that the wildfires destroyed orangutans' remaining habitat, and AFP reported on a new home being set up for rescued orangutans. TV5Monde reported that Gen Z was again on the streets, specifically protesting the fires and what they called a state of emergency in the country.

ECONOMY, MARKETS, AND TRADE. The economic picture was mixed. Indonesian stocks notched their best week since June on foreign buying (Bloomberg), yet the rupiah dropped to a record low on a strong dollar and MSCI-related concerns (Bloomberg). MSCI announced that Barito Pacific would be removed from its indexes and that Indonesia would cut 300 more tightly held stocks from its benchmark (Reuters, Bloomberg). Indonesia issued its second panda bond offering despite the MSCI threat (Bloomberg). The budget deficit stood at 1.5 percent of GDP for January through October (Reuters). On the trade and energy side, the president ordered a greater share of mining benefits for the state (Reuters), the DSI announced a single-digit dollar-a-ton export fee (Bloomberg), Chinese coal buyers balked at Indonesian miners' contract demands (Bloomberg), an Indonesian billionaire's LNG plant received 140 million dollars from Canada (Bloomberg), BP sold a 49.9 percent stake in an Indonesian petrol station venture (Reuters), and Norway agreed to buy carbon offsets from Indonesian power projects (Reuters). An Indonesian tycoon was reportedly weighing a bid for Eramet's nickel mine (Bloomberg). September retail sales rose 0.6 percent year over year (Reuters).

TECHNOLOGY AND AI. Meta, TikTok, and Google jointly pushed back on Indonesia's planned revisions to its AI copyright law (Reuters), a sign that the tech sector is becoming a more visible player in Jakarta's policy debates.

NATURAL DISASTER. A separate earthquake displaced nearly 13,000 people (Deutsche Welle), adding to the week's pile of crises.

PROTESTS AND PUBLIC SENTIMENT. Gen Z protesters were back in the streets, both over the fires and over what TV5Monde described as a state of emergency in the country. The AFP note about social media misrepresenting a protest salute suggests the public mood is volatile and the narrative around Prabowo is contested.
measurement.expected:
POLITICAL MANEUVERING AROUND THE VP VACANCY. Almost certain: the next week will be consumed by behind-the-scenes negotiations over who will replace Gibran as vice president, with the formal vote not until December 2. Expect intense lobbying in the upper house, public speculation about candidates, and further friction between the Prabowo camp and the Jokowi loyalists. The FT's warning of 'open warfare' among the elite suggests that the wiretapping scandal and the VP ouster will be used as political weapons in the coming days. Probable: at least one or two names will be floated publicly as candidates, and there will be parliamentary committee meetings or closed-door consultations reported by state and private media.

WIETAPPING CASE AND TREASON CHARGES. Probable: with police saying they have 'enough evidence' for treason charges, we should expect formal indictments or at least the filing of charges against one or more individuals in the coming days. The ex-police chief's alleged role as 'end user' makes him a likely target. Possible: a bug sweep or forensic review of presidential and ministerial offices, as Reuters reported Indonesia was considering. This could generate new leaks and further political drama. Unlikely: a full trial or conviction within this single week, but the procedural steps (formal complaint, court scheduling) are plausible.

WILDFIRES AND CLIMATE ENFORCEMENT. Almost certain: the government will follow through on revoking land rights for the eight firms, with official announcements and possibly legal proceedings. Probable: further public statements from scientists and environmental groups about the 2.9 million hectares lost and the 3,560 deaths, and continued Gen Z street protests, especially if new fire hotspots appear. Possible: a parliamentary question time or special committee session on the fires and the government's response. The orangutan rescue and habitat loss story will continue to draw international attention.

MARKETS AND MSCI. Almost certain: the MSCI index changes (Barito Pacific removal, 300 additional stock cuts) will take effect or be announced in the coming days, likely causing short-term volatility. Probable: the rupiah will remain under pressure given the record-low level and the strong dollar, though the best-week-since-June equity performance and the second panda bond issuance suggest some foreign appetite remains. Possible: the new export fee on certain commodities will be formally gazetted, and the mining-benefits-for-the-state order will generate industry responses.

TECH AND AI LAW. Possible: further public pushback from Meta, TikTok, and Google, or a government statement clarifying the AI copyright revisions. Unlikely: a full legislative vote on the AI law within this week, but a draft or consultation round is plausible.

EARTHQUAKE AFTERMATH. Probable: continued relief operations for the 13,000 displaced, with government and NGO coordination. Possible: a follow-up tremor or aftershock, which would dominate headlines temporarily.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES. A surprise cabinet reshuffle beyond the VP slot, a formal state-of-emergency declaration triggered by the fires, a new major earthquake or volcanic eruption, an unexpected foreign state visit by a G7 leader to discuss the carbon-offset deal or LNG investment, or a sudden rupiah intervention by the central bank.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON. A full impeachment of President Prabowo within this week, a general strike or nationwide shutdown, a military coup or palace intrigue beyond the political elite squabbling, a new war or border conflict with Malaysia or the Philippines, a central bank rate cut (more likely a hold or hike given the rupiah weakness), or the VP replacement being announced before the December 2 vote in the upper house.

delta.motion: The political crisis exploded outward between the two photographs. In the first image, the Vice President was weakening: his equivalency document had been voided, an inquiry was being set up, and the president-VP rivalry was 'spilling into public.' Five days later, Gibran Rakabuming Raka had resigned, the Jokowi-Prabowo alliance was described as fraying, and 120 lawmakers had filed an impeachment motion over his credentials. The motion was fast and decisive, turning a procedural bruise into a full change of government at the second chair. The wiretapping scandal, which in the first photo was still in its early investigative phase with a fourth suspect just named and treason merely 'floated,' had by the second photo hardened into confirmed treason charges, a named 'end user' in the ex-police chief, and a government considering bug sweeps and tighter controls on spy tools. The story grew from a personnel purge into a structural reckoning over who controls the security state. The wildfire crisis also intensified. The first photo showed haze drifting to neighbors, a helicopter crash, and Australia sending waterbombing aircraft. The second photo revealed the full scale: 2.9 million hectares burned, 3,560 deaths attributed to fire pollution in September alone, climate change confirmed as an amplifier, eight listed firms having their land rights revoked, and Gen Z back in the streets calling it a state of emergency. The environmental story grew from a regional diplomatic irritant into a domestic political and existential issue. On the economic front, the MSCI saga moved from anxiety and a 'went too far' comment to concrete action: Barito Pacific removed from indexes, 300 more tightly held stocks cut, the rupiah at a record low, and a second panda bond issued anyway. The story grew from a threat to a realized market restructuring. New stories appeared that had no trace in the first photo: an earthquake displacing 13,000 people, Meta, TikTok, and Google jointly pushing back on AI copyright law revisions, Norway buying carbon offsets from Indonesian power projects, a Canadian investment in an LNG plant, palm oil price fears for 2027, and Chinese coal buyers balking at contract demands. The former president's defamation trial, which was a visible subplot in the first photo, vanished entirely from the second. The 20,000 troops in Jakarta, a dramatic symbol of the first photo's tension, were no longer mentioned, suggesting they had been quietly withdrawn. The data-center water complaints, a growing story in the first photo, faded from the headlines, partly displaced by the broader tech-sector question of AI copyright. Garuda Indonesia's CFO departure, noted in the first photo, did not reappear. In short, the political axis sharpened and accelerated, the environmental axis deepened and humanized, the economic axis became more concrete and punitive, and several smaller stories either resolved or were simply drowned out by the larger ones.
delta.wind: The expectation that the wiretapping scandal would remain dominant was correct, but the form was different. The forecast said the parliamentary inquiry into the VP would enter active hearings and that at least one more senior official would be named. Both were true in spirit: the ex-police chief was confirmed as the end user and treason charges were pursued. But the inquiry was overtaken by the VP's actual resignation, which was listed only as 'possible but would be a shock.' That shock arrived on schedule. The expectation that the 20,000 troops would stay deployed for at least another week was wrong; they were no longer a headline by the second photo, implying a quiet withdrawal. The expectation that the former president's defamation trial would continue with further testimony was also wrong; it simply vanished from the news cycle, likely buried under the VP resignation. The forecast rated a full cabinet reshuffle as possible but not probable, and a VP impeachment as unlikely. The VP did not get impeached, but 120 lawmakers filed the motion, and the resignation achieved the same political effect. The wildfires expectation was broadly correct: the fires continued, the haze persisted, and the diplomatic friction with Singapore and Malaysia continued. But the forecast did not anticipate the scale of the human toll (3,560 deaths in September) or the concrete government action of revoking land rights from eight listed firms. The helicopter crash investigation was expected to yield preliminary findings by the weekend, but it did not surface as a separate story, suggesting it was absorbed into the broader fire narrative. On the economy, the expectation that the dollar bond sale would be completed was met in a different form: a second panda bond was issued. The expectation that MSCI would prompt a finance ministry reassurance statement was understated; MSCI itself took action by removing Barito Pacific and cutting 300 stocks, which is a more concrete and punitive step than a verbal defense. The expectation that the nickel enforcement would see another procedural step was met, but the story evolved into the president ordering a greater share of mining benefits for the state and a tycoon weighing a bid for Eramet's mine, which is a broader strategic shift. The Garuda CFO departure was expected to spark board discussion, but it did not reappear, suggesting the story was resolved or deemed minor. The data-center expectations were mostly correct in their mildness: no major new deal, no major outage, and the local water complaints did not escalate into a headline event. The VP's position was expected to see a formal set of questions tabled by the inquiry committee and a possible public confrontation in the National Assembly. The confrontation happened, but through resignation rather than debate. The no-confidence vote was rated unlikely before November 16, and indeed the VP resigned before a formal vote could occur. Among the less likely surprises, the VP resignation was the one that hit, confirming that the forecast's probability calibration was reasonable. The earthquake, the AI copyright law pushback from the big tech firms, the Norway carbon deal, and the Gen Z protest framing were all genuinely new and not on the expectation list. The social-media misrepresentation of a protest salute, noted by TV5Monde, was a small but telling sign that the narrative battle around Prabowo was getting messier and more contested than the forecast anticipated. Overall, the expectations were directionally correct on the major political and environmental themes but underestimated the speed of the VP's exit, overestimated the persistence of the troop deployment and the defamation trial, and did not anticipate the concrete MSCI index actions or the cluster of smaller trade and energy stories that filled the economic news cycle.
delta.driver: The force moving Indonesia from the first photograph to the second is a president using a security-state scandal to restructure his political coalition while the country simultaneously absorbs a climate-driven physical shock that keeps the public on edge. Prabowo's wiretapping of his own security apparatus gave him a legitimate-sounding reason to purge the police hierarchy and consolidate control over the instruments of state power. The Vice President's credential controversy, which in the first photo was a procedural wound, became in the second photo the pretext to end the Jokowi-Prabowo compact that had held the ruling coalition together since 2024. The two stories are not parallel; they are sequential. The wiretapping scandal weakened the security establishment that had been loyal to the old alliance, and the credential dispute provided the public-facing justification to remove the alliance's symbolic figurehead. Meanwhile, the wildfires, amplified by El Niño and confirmed by climate science, created a constant background of public anger and Gen Z mobilization that made any government misstep more visible and more costly. The MSCI index actions, the rupiah's record low, and the removal of Barito Pacific from benchmarks are the external market's verdict on the same internal instability: foreign capital is pricing in governance risk. The tech sector's pushback on AI copyright law and the data-center water disputes represent a third axis: Indonesia's ambition to be a digital and energy hub is colliding with the practical limits of its infrastructure and the appetite of its population. All three forces, the political realignment, the climate shock, and the market-and-tech friction, are pulling in the same direction, toward a more centralized, more contested, and more publicly scrutinized version of Prabowo's government.

crystal.forecast:
POLITICAL CONSOLIDATION AND THE VACUUM AT THE SECOND CHAIR. The dominant story of the coming week will be the political maneuvering that follows Gibran Rakabuming Raka's resignation. With the DP selection not until December 2, Prabowo has a two-week window to restructure his coalition, manage the 120-lawmaker impeachment motion (which is now procedurally awkward but politically useful as a bargaining chip), and signal to both the Jokowi camp and the opposition that the government is stable. I expect back-channel negotiations, possible public statements from Jokowi or his camp clarifying their position, and a series of cabinet-level consultations. The wiretapping treason charges will be in early legal process, with the ex-police chief's role as 'end user' generating continued scrutiny and possible further personnel changes in the security establishment. The government's consideration of bug sweeps and tighter spy-tool controls will likely become a concrete policy proposal. Confidence: high that this is the dominant axis; moderate that no single dramatic new shock (like a second resignation or a cabinet collapse) lands in this specific week, though the motion pattern says I should keep that probability higher than my instinct. The less likely surprise this motion makes more probable is a public, on-record statement from Jokowi himself, who has been the silent gravitational anchor of the alliance; his son's removal strips him of his main institutional stake, and the noise around the credential dispute and the social-media misrepresentation of the protest salute suggest the narrative battle is messy enough that he may feel compelled to speak. Confidence in that specific event: moderate, maybe 30 to 40 percent. I would not bet on a full cabinet reshuffle this week, a no-confidence vote against Prabowo, or the DP selection being pulled forward of December 2.

WIRETAPPING SCANDAL AND TREASON CHARGES. The treason charges are now formally in play. The next week will likely see the early procedural steps: the police or prosecution filing the formal charge sheet, the ex-police chief being formally questioned or appearing before a panel, and the political class sorting out who is implicated and who is not. The 'bug sweeps' and tighter controls on spy tools will move from consideration to at least a draft policy or a public announcement. The Financial Times' framing of 'open warfare' among the political elite is the right register to expect: this is not a clean legal process but a political one dressed in legal language. The entanglement with the VP resignation means the wiretapping story will continue to feed the narrative of a Prabowo government consolidating power. I expect at least one more senior figure to be named or to become the subject of public speculation. Confidence: high that the legal process advances; moderate that a second named suspect or a higher-level connection emerges. I would not bet on the case going to full trial within this week or on a dramatic revelation that implicates Prabowo himself directly.

WILDFIRES, CLIMATE, AND PUBLIC PRESSURE. The dry season and El Niño are still active, and the fires will continue. The 2.9-million-hectare burn and 3,560 deaths are now the baseline, and the government's revocation of land rights from eight listed firms will generate corporate and political pushback. I expect at least one of those firms to respond publicly, possibly through legal channels or lobbying. The Gen Z protest movement, which TV5Monde and AFP have documented, will likely continue in some form, especially if the government's response to the fires is seen as reactive rather than structural. The social-media misrepresentation of the protest salute suggests the narrative battlefield is contested and that the government may try to manage the story more actively. I expect the haze to continue drifting toward Singapore and Malaysia, keeping the bilateral friction alive. Confidence: high that the fires and their political consequences remain a major story; moderate that a new specific event (a fresh fire hotspot, a new death toll update, a corporate lawsuit) adds a new dimension. I would not bet on the fires going away before the dry season breaks, which is not expected within this week.

ECONOMY, MARKETS, AND THE MSCI AFTERMATH. The MSCI removal of Barito Pacific and the cutting of 300 tightly held stocks will have a continued market impact. The rupiah at a record low will pressure Bank Indonesia, and I expect the central bank to make at least one public statement or take a small intervention step to signal confidence. The second panda bond was issued, which is a positive signal, but the overall market narrative is one of governance risk being priced in. The president's order for a greater share of mining benefits for the state and the single-digit dollar-a-ton export fee will generate industry reaction, particularly from the coal and nickel sectors. The Chinese coal buyers' reluctance and the Eramet nickel mine bid speculation will continue. Confidence: moderate-high that the market remains volatile and the rupiah stays under pressure; moderate that Bank Indonesia takes a visible step. I would not bet on a dramatic market crash or a relief rally of more than a couple of percent within this week.

TECH, AI, AND THE DIGITAL HUB AMBITION. The joint pushback from Meta, TikTok, and Google on Indonesia's AI copyright law revisions is a new and potentially growing story. I expect the government to respond, either with a clarifying statement, a revised draft, or a public debate in parliament. The data-center water complaints, which faded last week, could resurface if the big-tech pushback draws more public attention to the digital infrastructure question. Confidence: moderate that the AI copyright story generates at least one more headline; low that it becomes the dominant story. I would not bet on a major new data-center deal or a dramatic government concession on the copyright law within this week.

WHAT I WOULD NOT BET ON. A full cabinet reshuffle before the December 2 DP selection. A no-confidence vote against Prabowo. A state of emergency declaration. The former president's defamation trial reappearing as a headline. A second VP resignation or a dramatic new political shock beyond the wiretapping and coalition realignment already in motion. A major new natural disaster (earthquake, flood) that displaces the existing stories. The rupiah collapsing by more than 3 to 4 percent in a single week. A full reversal of the MSCI actions.
crystal.headline: Prabowo Navigates Post-Gibran Vacuum as Treason Charges Advance
emoji_reasons: The Vice President's resignation and the fracturing of the Jokowi-Prabowo alliance are the week's defining political drama, with coalition maneuvering, an impeachment motion, and a two-week vacancy at the second chair.
Confirmed treason charges from the wiretapping scandal, the ex-police chief named as end user, and early legal proceedings put the justice system at the center of the political story.
The 2.9-million-hectare wildfire crisis, 3,560 attributed deaths, Gen Z protests, and corporate pushback over land-right revocations keep the environmental and social-instability axis burning.
crystal.tldr: Indonesia's next week will be dominated by the political maneuvering that follows Vice President Gibran's resignation, with Prabowo working to stabilize his coalition before the December 2 selection of a new VP, while the wiretapping treason charges enter early legal process. The wildfire crisis, Gen Z protests, and MSCI-driven market jitters will continue as persistent secondary pressures. Expect back-channel negotiations, a possible public statement from the former President Jokowi, and continued rupiah weakness, but no full cabinet reshuffle or dramatic new political shock within this specific week.
crystal.eli5:
Imagine a team where the captain and the co-captain have been best friends for a while, but the co-captain just quit in the middle of the season. That is basically what happened in Indonesia. The Vice President, who is the son of the former President, resigned last week, and now the current President has to figure out how to run his team without his best friend's son in the co-captain seat. The new person will not be chosen until early December, so for the next two weeks it is all backroom deals, whispered conversations, and trying to make sure nobody else quits.

At the same time, there is a spy scandal. It turns out that the President's own security people were secretly recording his phone calls, and now they are formally charging the top police officer with treason, which is like saying he betrayed the country. This is a big deal because it means the President is cleaning up his own security team, and everyone in politics is watching to see who else gets caught up in it. Think of it like a school where the principal finds out the vice principal was secretly recording the teachers, and now the principal is deciding who stays and who goes.

On top of all the political drama, the forests in the big islands of Sumatra and Kalimantan are still on fire. A lot of them. Like, a really, really big amount. The smoke is so bad that it blew over to Singapore and Malaysia, and people in those countries are not happy. About 3,500 people died in September just from breathing the smoky air, and the government is now taking away land permits from eight big companies that they blame for the fires. Those companies are not going to be quiet about it. And the young people, the Gen Z crowd, are back on the streets protesting, saying the government is not doing enough. So the next week in Indonesia is going to be a lot of political back-and-forth, some legal drama, a lot of smoke, and a stock market that is nervous about all of it.

The wildfire and haze persistence was accurately called, as was the diplomatic friction with neighbors. The forecast correctly noted the VP's equivalency document would be cited in debate and that the inquiry committee would table formal questions (120 lawmakers filed impeachment). However, Forecast A explicitly rated the VP being 'formally impeached or removed' as 'unlikely this week' and listed a sudden VP resignation as a 'less likely surprise' that 'would be a shock.' The VP's resignation was the single biggest story of the week, so this was a notable under-call on scale.
